meta.session_title: Day 1 - Introduction to Java & Language Fundamentals
meta.pedagogy: Hands-on learning with step-by-step guidance. Each exercise builds on the previous. All concepts from the session are coded. Banking/finance examples used for context.

objectives: Apply all major operator types: arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, increment/decrement, and ternary to build real calculation logic.
prerequisites: IntelliJ IDEA (Community Edition) or VS Code with Java Extension
Git installed and GitHub account created

exercises.title: Operators — Interest & EMI Calculator
exercises.objective: Apply all major operator types: arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, increment/decrement, and ternary to build real calculation logic.
exercises.scenario: RoboBank needs a quick interest and loan eligibility calculator. You'll build it using Java operators.
instructions: Step 1: Create class 'OperatorsDemo' in your project
Step 2: Implement each section of the starter code, replacing TODO comments
Step 3: Run and verify all outputs
Step 4: Experiment with changing values and predict the output BEFORE running
Step 5: Complete the CHALLENGE at the bottom

hints: Math.pow(base, exp) computes base^exp. Example: Math.pow(1.09, 3) = 1.295...
The % operator gives the remainder. 847293 % 10 gives the last digit (3).
EMI formula: Math.pow(1 + monthlyRate, months) is used twice — compute it once and store in a variable
reflection_questions: What would happen if annualRate were 0? Would compound interest formula break? Test it.
When would you prefer ternary operator over if-else? When would you prefer if-else?
The compound interest formula uses Math.pow(). What is the Java equivalent of 2^10? Write it.
exercises.debugging_task: Introduce this bug: double monthlyRate = 9 / 12; instead of 0.09 / 12. What value does monthlyRate get? Why? (Hint: integer division!) How do you fix it?
